title: Introduction to Literary Studies
description: How to read literature closely and write about it well: the elements of fiction, poetry, and drama; close reading and annotation; interpretation and evidence; and the conventions of the literary essay.
outcomes: Read literary texts closely, attending to diction, imagery, figurative language, tone, and syntax.
Analyze plot, conflict, character, point of view, and setting in fiction.
Interpret themes, symbols, motifs, and ambiguity.
Read drama as both text and performance.
Weigh historical, biographical, and reader-centered contexts in interpretation.
Write and cite arguable, evidence-based literary essays.

weeks.title: Why Read Literature?
weeks.overview: What literature is, how literary reading differs from reading for information, and the habits of attention that make it rewarding.
objectives: Distinguish literary reading from reading for information.
Describe the major genres of literature.
Practice annotation as a tool for close attention.
weeks.lesson:
## A different kind of reading

Most of the reading we do each day is for information: a news story, an email, instructions, a lesson like this one. We read quickly, extract what we need, and move on. Literature asks for something else. A poem, story, novel, or play isn't simply a container for a message that could be summarized and discarded. *How* it says something is part of *what* it says.

Consider the opening of Charles Dickens's *A Tale of Two Cities* (1859):

> It was the best of times, it was the worst of times…

As information, the sentence says: the period had good and bad aspects. As literature, it does much more. The balanced, repeated structure enacts the contradictions of the age it describes. The rhythm is incantatory, almost biblical. And the paradox, both best and worst at once, plunges us into a novel about revolution, doubleness, and the coexistence of opposites. Paraphrase loses all of that.

## What counts as literature?

There's no definition everyone accepts. Literature is often described as writing valued for its artistry and its exploration of human experience, writing in which language does more than convey facts. The boundaries have shifted over time: novels were once considered light entertainment, and works by women, people of color, and writers outside Europe were long excluded from "the canon" of works deemed worthy of study. Literary studies today reads widely and asks how judgments of value are made.

## The major genres

- **Fiction:** invented narratives in prose, from short stories to novels.
- **Poetry:** writing that uses compressed language, rhythm, sound, and the line as essential tools.
- **Drama:** writing meant to be performed, told through dialogue and action.
- **Literary nonfiction:** essays, memoir, and other true writing crafted with literary art.

Genres blend and overlap: prose poems, novels in verse, plays that read like poems.

## Why read it?

- **To experience other lives.** Literature lets us inhabit minds unlike our own, across time, place, and circumstance.
- **To think more precisely.** Close reading trains attention to nuance, ambiguity, and implication, skills useful everywhere.
- **To understand our cultures.** Literature records how people have understood love, death, power, faith, and justice.
- **For pleasure.** Delight in language, suspense, beauty, and humor is a reason in itself.

## Reading slowly: annotation

The most important habit in this program is **annotation**: marking a text as you read. Underline striking words, note questions in the margins, mark repetitions and patterns, and record your reactions. Annotation turns reading from passive reception into active conversation.

Useful things to mark:

- Words that surprise you or seem chosen with special care.
- **Repetitions** and **patterns**: of words, images, sounds, or situations.
- Shifts in tone, speaker, or time.
- Moments of confusion. Confusion is often where the most interesting interpretation begins.

### Worked example: annotating an opening

The first sentence of Jane Austen's *Pride and Prejudice* (1813):

> It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.

Annotations might note: "universally acknowledged" sounds grand, even philosophical, but the "truth" is gossip; the sentence is **ironic**. Who really "wants" here? In the world of the novel, it's the families of unmarried daughters who want the rich single man. The sentence's form, a pompous generalization, mocks the society it describes. In one line, Austen establishes her ironic voice and her central subjects: marriage, money, and social pressure.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Literature has one hidden meaning the teacher knows."** Good interpretations are arguments supported by evidence; several can be valid.
- **"Analyzing a work ruins it."** Close attention usually deepens enjoyment.
- **"Only old books count as literature."** Literature includes contemporary and global writing in every form.

## Summary

Literary reading attends to how language works, not just what it says. Literature spans fiction, poetry, drama, and literary nonfiction, and what counts as literature has changed over time. Annotation is the essential habit of close, active reading.

keyTerms.definition: Reading that attends to how language and form create meaning, not only to information.
A category of literature, such as fiction, poetry, drama, or literary nonfiction.
The body of works traditionally considered most worthy of study, whose boundaries are debated.
Marking and commenting on a text while reading.
A gap between what is said and what is meant, or between expectation and reality.

weeks.title: Close Reading: Language and Imagery
weeks.overview: The foundational skill of literary study: reading closely for diction, imagery, figurative language, tone, and syntax.
objectives: Analyze diction and connotation.
Identify imagery and figurative language and explain their effects.
Describe tone and how syntax contributes to meaning.
weeks.lesson:
## The building blocks

**Close reading** is careful, sustained attention to the language of a text: the specific words, images, and sentences, and how they work together. It is the foundation of everything in literary studies.

## Diction and connotation

**Diction** is word choice. Every word has a **denotation** (its dictionary meaning) and **connotations** (associations and feelings). "Home," "house," and "residence" denote similar things but connote very different ones: warmth, a building, officialdom.

Writers choose words for sound, rhythm, register (formal or informal), and connotation. When you read, ask: Why this word and not another?

## Imagery

**Imagery** is language that appeals to the senses: sight, sound, smell, taste, touch, and motion. Images make writing concrete and vivid, and they often carry meaning beyond the literal.

In Kate Chopin's "The Story of an Hour" (1894), a woman who has just learned of her husband's death sits by an open window:

> She could see in the open square before her house the tops of trees that were all aquiver with the new spring life.

The images of spring, new life, and an open window come at a moment when we might expect grief. They prepare us for the story's surprising turn, and they suggest what she is beginning to feel.

## Figurative language

**Figurative language** departs from literal meaning to create comparison and association:

- **Simile:** an explicit comparison using "like" or "as." ("I wandered lonely as a cloud," Wordsworth.)
- **Metaphor:** an implied comparison, saying one thing *is* another. ("All the world's a stage," Shakespeare.)
- **Personification:** giving human qualities to non-human things.
- **Symbol:** an object or image that stands for something beyond itself (more in Week 5).

Figures of speech do more than decorate. A metaphor makes us see one thing *as* another, and the comparison carries implications.

## Tone

**Tone** is the attitude a text conveys toward its subject or audience: affectionate, ironic, bitter, playful, solemn. Tone arises from diction, imagery, and rhythm together. Misreading tone, taking irony as sincerity, for example, can turn an interpretation upside down.

## Syntax

**Syntax** is sentence structure. Long, flowing sentences can create a sense of abundance or breathless rush; short, clipped ones, of tension or finality. Repetition, parallelism, and the placement of words at the start or end of a sentence create emphasis.

The first sentence of Herman Melville's *Moby-Dick* (1851) is just three words: "Call me Ishmael." Its brevity and directness contrast with the vast, digressive novel that follows, and its oddly indirect phrasing ("call me," not "my name is") raises questions about the narrator from the start.

### Worked example: close reading a passage

From "The Story of an Hour," after Mrs. Mallard begins to feel something approaching:

> She said it over and over under her breath: "free, free, free!"

*Diction:* "free," a word we don't expect from a new widow. *Repetition:* three times, building intensity. *Syntax:* the phrase stands alone, unexplained. *Tone:* the narration doesn't judge her; it observes. Together these choices dramatize a hidden longing, and they invite readers to think about what marriage meant for women in Chopin's time.

## Moving from observation to interpretation

Close reading has two steps:
1. **Observe:** notice patterns, choices, and details.
2. **Interpret:** explain what they mean and why they matter.

A list of devices isn't an interpretation. "The author uses imagery" is an observation; "The images of spring life suggest Mrs. Mallard's grief is mixed with a sense of renewal she can barely admit" is an interpretation.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Identifying devices is the goal."** The goal is explaining their effects and meaning.
- **"Authors don't really intend all these details."** Whether or not every effect was planned, the words on the page create meaning readers can analyze.
- **"Tone is the same as mood."** Tone is the text's attitude; mood is the feeling it creates in readers.

## Summary

Close reading examines diction and connotation, imagery, figurative language, tone, and syntax. Its essential move is from observing patterns to interpreting what they mean.

keyTerms.definition: An author's choice of words.
The associations and feelings a word carries beyond its literal meaning.
Language that appeals to the senses.
An implied comparison stating that one thing is another.
The attitude a text conveys toward its subject or audience.

weeks.title: Plot, Structure, and Conflict
weeks.overview: How stories are built: plot and story, conflict, the shape of narrative, and the manipulation of time.
objectives: Distinguish story from plot and analyze narrative structure.
Identify types of conflict and their role in a narrative.
Explain how manipulations of time, such as flashback and foreshadowing, shape meaning.
weeks.lesson:
## Story and plot

Narrative theorists distinguish between **story**, the events in chronological order, and **plot** (or discourse), the way those events are arranged and presented in the telling. E. M. Forster offered a famous illustration: "The king died and then the queen died" is a story; "The king died, and then the queen died of grief" is a plot, because it introduces causation.

A writer can tell the same story many ways: beginning at the end, withholding key information, jumping between times, or telling it through different characters. These choices shape suspense, sympathy, and meaning.

## Conflict

Most narratives turn on **conflict**, a struggle between opposing forces. Common types:

- **Character versus character:** a rivalry, a villain.
- **Character versus society:** a person against laws, norms, or institutions.
- **Character versus nature:** a storm, a wilderness, illness.
- **Character versus self:** an internal struggle with desire, fear, or conscience.

Most rich stories combine several. In "The Story of an Hour," the central conflict is internal, but it is shaped by social expectations about marriage, so it also involves society.

## The shape of a plot

A traditional model, often associated with the nineteenth-century critic Gustav Freytag and visualized as a pyramid, divides plot into:

1. **Exposition:** introducing characters, setting, and situation.
2. **Rising action:** complications that build tension.
3. **Climax:** the turning point of greatest intensity.
4. **Falling action:** consequences unfold.
5. **Resolution** (or *dénouement*): a new equilibrium.

Many stories, especially modern short stories, don't follow this shape neatly. Some end at the climax; some withhold resolution; some are built around a moment of realization rather than external action. James Joyce used the word **epiphany** for such a sudden moment of insight.

## Time

Writers manipulate time to create effects:

- **Flashback:** presenting earlier events after later ones.
- **Foreshadowing:** hints of what is to come.
- **In medias res:** beginning "in the middle of things," as many epics do.
- **Pacing:** expanding a moment over pages or compressing years into a sentence.

### Worked example: structure and surprise in "The Story of an Hour"

The story's plot is compressed into a single hour. Its opening sentence foreshadows the ending: Mrs. Mallard is "afflicted with a heart trouble," so the news of her husband's death is broken to her gently. The rising action is internal: alone in her room, she moves from grief to a dawning, exhilarating sense of freedom. The climax arrives when her husband walks through the door, alive. In the final sentence, the doctors say she died "of the joy that kills."

The structure creates dramatic irony. The doctors believe she died of joy at seeing him; readers, who have been inside her room, suspect the opposite. The plot's brevity and its final reversal force us to reconsider everything we have read.

## Endings

Endings carry special weight. A **closed** ending resolves the conflict; an **open** ending leaves questions unresolved. A **twist** ending reverses expectations; when done well, it makes us reread the whole story differently, rather than merely surprising us.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Plot is just what happens."** Plot is how events are arranged and connected.
- **"Every story follows Freytag's pyramid."** Many modern stories deliberately don't.
- **"A twist ending is the point of a story."** The best twists illuminate what came before.

## Summary

Story is chronology; plot is arrangement and causation. Conflict drives narrative, whether external or internal. Traditional structure moves from exposition to resolution, though many stories break that pattern. Writers manipulate time through flashback, foreshadowing, and pacing to create meaning.

keyTerms.definition: The arrangement and causal connection of events in a narrative.
A struggle between opposing forces that drives a narrative.
The turning point of greatest tension in a plot.
A sudden moment of insight or realization, a term associated with James Joyce.
Hints or clues that suggest what will happen later.

weeks.title: Character, Point of View, and Setting
weeks.overview: Who acts, who tells, and where: characterization, narrative perspective, reliability, and setting as a force in fiction.
objectives: Analyze methods of characterization, including round and flat characters.
Identify point of view and evaluate narrative reliability.
Explain how setting shapes character and meaning.
weeks.lesson:
## Character

**Characters** are the people (or beings) of fiction. Writers create them through:

- **Direct characterization:** the narrator tells us what a character is like.
- **Indirect characterization:** we infer character from actions, speech, thoughts, appearance, and how others respond.

Indirect characterization is usually more powerful, because readers participate in the inference. "Show, don't tell" is a familiar writers' maxim for this reason.

E. M. Forster distinguished **round** characters, complex and capable of surprising us convincingly, from **flat** characters, built around a single idea or quality. Flat characters aren't failures; they serve purposes, such as comedy or contrast. A **dynamic** character changes over the course of a narrative; a **static** one doesn't.

## Point of view

**Point of view** is the perspective from which a story is told. The **narrator** is the voice telling it, which is not the same as the author.

- **First person:** a character narrates, using "I." We get intimacy and immediacy but only what that character knows and chooses to reveal.
- **Third person limited:** the narrator uses "he" or "she" but stays close to one character's perceptions and thoughts.
- **Third person omniscient:** the narrator knows and can reveal the thoughts of many characters, and may comment on the action.
- **Free indirect discourse:** a third-person narration that slips into a character's own idiom and thoughts without quotation marks, blending narrator and character. Jane Austen was a pioneer of this technique.
- **Second person:** "you," rare but striking.

## Reliability

An **unreliable narrator** is one whose account readers have reason to doubt, because the narrator is deceptive, self-deceiving, naive, biased, or mentally disturbed. Unreliable narration creates **dramatic irony**: readers understand more than the narrator does.

### Worked example: "The Tell-Tale Heart"

Poe's narrator opens by insisting on his sanity:

> True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?

His frantic punctuation, his obsession with the old man's "vulture eye," and the calm pride with which he describes a murder all contradict his claim. The more he argues for his sanity, the less we believe him. The story's horror comes from inhabiting a mind that cannot see itself, and its final confession, provoked by the imagined beating of the dead man's heart, reveals guilt the narrator never admits.

## Setting

**Setting** is the time, place, and social environment of a story. It can be:

- **Backdrop:** a location where events happen.
- **Atmosphere:** creating mood, as in Gothic fiction's dark, decaying houses.
- **Social world:** the norms, classes, and pressures that shape characters' choices.
- **Symbol:** a place that carries meaning, such as a garden, a city, or a border.

In James Joyce's "Araby" (1914), a boy's dreams of a romantic, "Eastern" bazaar collide with the dim, dead-end streets of turn-of-the-century Dublin. When he finally reaches the bazaar, it is closing, its lights going out, and the setting's disappointment becomes his own. The story ends with an epiphany:

> I saw myself as a creature driven and derided by vanity; and my eyes burned with anguish and anger.

## How the elements interact

Character, point of view, and setting work together. A first-person narrator's limited perspective shapes how we see the setting; a setting's social pressures shape a character's options; an omniscient narrator's commentary shapes our judgment of characters. Analyzing fiction means seeing how these elements combine.

## Common misconceptions

- **"The narrator is the author."** The narrator is a constructed voice.
- **"Flat characters are badly written."** They serve deliberate purposes.
- **"Setting is just background."** Setting often shapes character and meaning.

## Summary

Writers create characters directly and indirectly; characters may be round or flat, dynamic or static. Point of view determines what readers can know, and unreliable narrators create dramatic irony. Setting can be backdrop, atmosphere, social world, or symbol, and all these elements interact.

A complex character capable of surprising the reader convincingly.
A narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt.
Third-person narration that takes on a character's own voice and thoughts.
The time, place, and social environment of a narrative.

weeks.title: Theme, Symbol, and Interpretation
weeks.overview: What a work means: themes as arguments rather than topics, symbols and motifs, ambiguity, and building an interpretation from evidence.
objectives: Distinguish a topic from a theme and articulate themes as claims.
Analyze symbols and motifs.
Develop and defend an interpretation that accounts for ambiguity.
weeks.lesson:
## Topic versus theme

A **topic** is a subject: love, death, freedom, ambition. A **theme** is what a work suggests *about* a topic, a claim or insight that can be stated as a sentence.

- *Topic:* marriage.
- *Theme:* "The Story of an Hour" suggests that even a kind marriage can confine a woman's sense of self in a society that offers her no independent identity.

Themes are rarely stated outright. Readers infer them from the work's patterns: what happens, how characters change, which images recur, and how the work ends. A rich work usually has several themes, sometimes in tension with each other.

## Symbol

A **symbol** is an object, image, character, or action that carries meaning beyond its literal sense. Some symbols are **conventional**, widely shared in a culture (a dove for peace, a skull for death). Others are **contextual**, created within a particular work.

A symbol isn't a code with one correct answer. It gathers meanings through its context in the work. The open window in "The Story of an Hour" is literally a window, but in context it suggests possibility, the world beyond the house, and the freedom Mrs. Mallard imagines.

## Motif

A **motif** is a recurring element, an image, phrase, situation, or idea, that develops meaning through repetition. Tracking motifs is one of the most reliable ways to find a work's themes. In "Araby," light and darkness recur throughout: dark streets, the faint light of shop windows, the glow the boy associates with the girl, and finally the darkness as the bazaar closes.

### Worked example: "The Gift of the Magi"

O. Henry's story (1905) follows a poor young couple, Della and Jim, each of whom sells a treasured possession to buy the other a Christmas gift. Della sells her long hair to buy a chain for Jim's watch; Jim sells his watch to buy combs for her hair. The gifts are now useless.

- *Topic:* love, sacrifice, gifts.
- *Possible theme:* True generosity lies in the willingness to sacrifice, not in the usefulness of what is given.
- *Symbols:* Della's hair and Jim's watch, their most prized possessions, stand for the self each is willing to give up.
- *Title:* the Magi, the wise men who brought gifts to the infant Jesus. The narrator calls the couple foolish, then insists that of all who give gifts, such people are the wisest. The irony is gentle and affirming.

## Ambiguity

Many great works are **ambiguous**: they support more than one reasonable interpretation. Ambiguity isn't vagueness; it's a richness of meaning that invites debate. Is Mrs. Mallard's death a punishment, a tragedy, a release? The story supports several readings, and part of its power lies in that.

## Building an interpretation

A strong interpretation:

1. **Makes a claim** about meaning that isn't obvious.
2. **Uses evidence**, especially quotations, from the text.
3. **Accounts for patterns**: motifs, structure, symbols.
4. **Addresses complications**: details that seem to cut against it.
5. **Explains significance**: why the reading matters.

Interpretations can be judged. One that ignores much of the text, or relies on details that aren't there, is weaker than one that accounts for more of the evidence.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Theme is a single word like 'love.'"** That's a topic; a theme is a claim about it.
- **"Every object in a story is a symbol."** Symbols earn their meaning through emphasis, pattern, and context.
- **"If a work is ambiguous, any reading goes."** Interpretations must be supported by the text.

## Summary

Themes are claims a work suggests about its topics. Symbols and motifs gather meaning through context and repetition. Ambiguity enriches literature, and strong interpretations make non-obvious claims grounded in textual evidence while addressing complications.

keyTerms.definition: An insight or claim a work suggests about a topic.
An element that carries meaning beyond its literal sense.
A recurring element that develops meaning through repetition.
The capacity of a text to support more than one reasonable interpretation.
An argument about a text's meaning, supported by textual evidence.

quiz.prompt: Which is a theme rather than a topic?
choices: Ambition, pursued without limits, destroys what it seeks to gain
quiz.explanation: A theme is a claim about a topic.

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes a motif from a single symbol?
choices: A motif is always a color
A motif is the work's title
A motif recurs throughout a work, developing meaning through repetition
quiz.explanation: Repetition is what makes a motif.

quiz.prompt: In "The Gift of the Magi," Della's hair and Jim's watch function primarily as:
choices: Symbols of what each is willing to sacrifice for the other
quiz.explanation: Their most prized possessions represent their selves.

quiz.prompt: What makes an interpretation stronger than another?
choices: It accounts for more of the textual evidence, including complications
It is more surprising regardless of evidence
quiz.explanation: Interpretations are judged by how well they fit the text.

quiz.prompt: A literary work that supports several reasonable readings is described as:
quiz.explanation: Ambiguity is a richness of meaning.

assignment.title: Interpret a Story
assignment.prompt:
Choose one story we've discussed ("The Story of an Hour," "The Tell-Tale Heart," "The Gift of the Magi," or "Araby").

weeks.title: Reading Drama
weeks.overview: Plays as literature and performance: dialogue, stage directions, dramatic irony, and the conventions of tragedy and comedy, with Susan Glaspell's Trifles.
objectives: Explain how drama differs from fiction as a written form.
Analyze dialogue, stage directions, and dramatic irony.
Describe the conventions of tragedy and comedy.
weeks.lesson:
## Words meant for bodies and voices

A play is written to be performed. On the page, a drama consists mostly of **dialogue** and **stage directions**, without the narrator who in fiction tells us what characters think and how to judge them. Readers of drama must imagine performance: how lines are spoken, what silences mean, how characters move and look at each other.

## Elements of drama

- **Dialogue:** characters reveal themselves through what they say, and what they don't.
- **Monologue:** an extended speech by one character to others.
- **Soliloquy:** a speech in which a character, alone or unheard, voices private thoughts to the audience. Hamlet's "To be, or not to be, that is the question" is the most famous example in English.
- **Aside:** a brief remark to the audience that other characters don't hear.
- **Stage directions:** the playwright's instructions about setting, action, and manner.
- **Subtext:** what lies beneath the dialogue, the unspoken meanings and motives.

## Dramatic irony

**Dramatic irony** occurs when the audience knows something the characters don't. It creates tension, comedy, or tragic pity. In Sophocles' *Oedipus the King*, the audience knows from the start the truth Oedipus is determined to uncover, that he himself killed his father and married his mother, so every confident line he speaks carries a terrible double meaning.

## Tragedy and comedy

Since antiquity, drama has been organized around two broad modes.

**Tragedy** traditionally depicts the downfall of a significant figure. Aristotle, in his *Poetics*, described tragedy as arousing **pity and fear** and producing **catharsis**, often understood as a purging or clarification of those emotions. The tragic hero often has a **hamartia**, sometimes translated as a "tragic flaw" but closer to an error in judgment.

**Comedy** traditionally moves from confusion toward harmony, often ending in reconciliation or marriage. It may satirize social follies, as in Molière, or delight in romantic complication, as in Shakespeare's comedies.

Many modern plays blend modes or reject them, and **realism** in the late nineteenth century, associated with Henrik Ibsen, brought ordinary middle-class lives and social problems to the stage.

### Worked example: Susan Glaspell's *Trifles* (1916)

In this one-act play, a farmer, John Wright, has been found strangled in his bed, and his wife, Minnie, is suspected. The county attorney and sheriff search the house for evidence of a motive, while their wives, Mrs. Hale and Mrs. Peters, wait in the kitchen. The men mock the women's concern with "trifles," domestic details such as quilting and preserves.

But it is the women who solve the case. Through small details, such as erratic stitching on a quilt, a broken birdcage, and finally a dead canary with its neck wrung, they reconstruct Minnie's isolated, joyless life and her motive. In the end, they conceal the evidence from the men.

*Dramatic irony:* the audience watches the women understand what the men cannot see, even as the men condescend to them. *Stage directions and subtext:* silences, glances, and gestures between the women carry crucial meaning. *Title:* the "trifles" the men dismiss are exactly what matter. *Theme:* the play exposes how women's lives and knowledge were overlooked in a world run by men, and asks whose justice the law serves.

## Reading a play

When reading drama:

1. Read the stage directions carefully; they are part of the text.
2. Imagine the performance: tone of voice, movement, silence.
3. Track what characters want and what stands in their way.
4. Notice what isn't said.
5. Consider how different productions might interpret the same lines.

## Common misconceptions

- **"Stage directions can be skipped."** They often carry essential meaning.
- **"Tragic heroes are destroyed by a single character flaw."** Aristotle's hamartia is more an error of judgment, and many tragedies emphasize circumstances and fate.
- **"Comedy is less serious than tragedy."** Comedy often offers sharp social criticism.

## Summary

Drama is written for performance and works through dialogue, stage directions, and subtext. Soliloquies and asides reveal inner lives; dramatic irony lets the audience know more than the characters. Tragedy and comedy offer traditional shapes, and *Trifles* shows how a short realist play can use dramatic irony to expose a whole social order.

A playwright's instructions about setting, action, and manner of delivery.
A situation in which the audience knows something the characters do not.
In Aristotle's account of tragedy, the purging or clarification of pity and fear.
The unspoken meanings and motives beneath dialogue.

weeks.title: Text and Context
weeks.overview: Reading literature in relation to authors, history, and readers: biographical and historical context, the intentional fallacy, and reader response.
objectives: Explain how historical and biographical context can inform interpretation.
Describe debates about authorial intention.
Explain how readers and reading communities shape meaning.
weeks.lesson:
## The text and its worlds

So far we've focused on the text itself: its language, structure, and form. But literature is made by people, in particular times and places, and read by others in different times and places. How much should context shape interpretation? Literary critics have argued about this for a century.

## Formalism and close reading

In the mid-twentieth century, critics associated with the **New Criticism** argued that a poem or story should be read as a self-contained work of art. Meaning lies in the words on the page: their tensions, ironies, and patterns. This approach gave us the discipline of close reading you've been practicing.

## The intentional fallacy

In a famous 1946 essay, W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley argued against the **intentional fallacy**: the error, as they saw it, of judging a work by what its author intended. The author's intention, they argued, is often unknowable, and in any case the work means what its words mean, not what its author hoped. If a poem achieves its aims, the poem shows it; if it doesn't, the author's intentions can't rescue it.

Others disagree, arguing that understanding what an author was trying to do, through letters, drafts, and biography, legitimately illuminates a work. Most critics today take a middle position: authors' intentions and lives are evidence worth considering, but they don't settle what a work means.

## Historical context

Knowing a work's historical moment can be essential. "The Story of an Hour," published in 1894, appeared when married women in the United States had limited legal and economic independence, and debates about "the woman question" were intense. That context deepens our understanding of Mrs. Mallard's "free, free, free!" Without it, we might misread her as simply callous.

Historical context also helps us avoid **anachronism**, reading old words with modern meanings, and helps us see how a work responded to its own world: whether it challenged, reinforced, or complicated the assumptions of its time.

## Biographical context

An author's life can illuminate a work, but with care. Kate Chopin was widowed young and raised six children; it is tempting to read her own life into her stories. But a story is a crafted fiction, not a confession, and treating it as autobiography can flatten it.

## Readers and reception

**Reader-response** critics emphasize that meaning arises in the encounter between text and reader. Readers bring experiences, expectations, and assumptions that shape what they notice and how they interpret. Different **interpretive communities**, in the critic Stanley Fish's phrase, read in different ways.

**Reception history** studies how a work has been read over time. Many works have been reinterpreted dramatically: Herman Melville's *Moby-Dick* sold poorly and was largely neglected for decades before critics in the early twentieth century hailed it as a masterpiece. A work's meaning is not fixed at the moment of publication.

## Critical approaches

In Literary Theory and Criticism (LIT 201) you will study approaches in depth. A preview:

| Approach | Central question |
|---|---|
| Formalist | How do the work's language and form create meaning? |
| Historicist | How does the work engage its historical moment? |
| Feminist | How does the work represent gender and power? |
| Marxist | How does the work reflect and shape class and economic relations? |
| Postcolonial | How does the work engage empire, colonialism, and their legacies? |
| Psychoanalytic | What desires and anxieties does the work express? |
| Ecocritical | How does the work represent nature and the environment? |

These are lenses, not rival religions. Each brings different features into focus.

### Worked example: two lenses on *Trifles*

A **feminist** reading emphasizes how the play exposes the dismissal of women's knowledge and the isolation of rural farm wives. A **historicist** reading notes that the play was written before American women had won the national vote, when women typically could not serve on juries, which sharpens the question of who gets to judge Minnie Wright. Both readings illuminate the play; together they're richer than either alone.

## Common misconceptions

- **"The author's intention is the true meaning."** Intention is evidence, not a final verdict.
- **"Context doesn't matter; only the text does."** Context can prevent misreadings and deepen interpretation.
- **"Reader response means any reading is valid."** Readings must still answer to the text.

## Summary

Critics debate how much context should shape interpretation. Formalists emphasize the text itself; the intentional fallacy warns against equating meaning with intention. Historical and biographical context can illuminate works, readers and communities shape meaning, and a work's reception changes over time. Critical approaches are lenses that reveal different aspects of a text.

keyTerms.definition: A mid-twentieth-century approach emphasizing close reading of the text as a self-contained work.
The claimed error of judging a work's meaning by its author's intentions.
The circumstances of the time in which a work was written or set.
An approach emphasizing the reader's role in making meaning.
The study of how a work has been read and valued over time.

weeks.title: Writing About Literature
weeks.overview: Turning reading into argument: literary theses, using quotations, structuring an essay, MLA citation, and the scholarly conversation.
objectives: Write an arguable, specific literary thesis.
Integrate and analyze quotations effectively.
Structure and cite a literary essay in MLA style.
weeks.lesson:
## The literary essay

A literary essay is an **argument about a text**: a claim about its meaning or workings, supported with evidence from the text and reasoning about that evidence. It is not a plot summary or a review saying whether you liked it. Your reader is assumed to have read the work; your job is to show them something they might not have seen.

## The literary thesis

A strong literary thesis:

- **Makes an arguable claim** about meaning, not a factual statement.
- **Is specific**, naming the elements you'll analyze.
- **Answers "how" or "why,"** not just "what."
- **Matters**, revealing something significant about the work.

| Weak | Strong |
|---|---|
| "The Story of an Hour" is about a woman whose husband dies. | In "The Story of an Hour," Chopin uses images of open windows and spring renewal to suggest that Mrs. Mallard's true grief is not for her husband but for the self her marriage has suppressed. |
| *Trifles* has a lot of irony. | Glaspell's *Trifles* turns the men's contempt for "trifles" into the play's central irony, revealing that the knowledge they dismiss is the only path to understanding Minnie Wright's crime. |

## Using quotations

Literary essays live on quotations. Use them well:

1. **Introduce** the quotation, giving context.
2. **Quote** precisely and briefly, often just a phrase.
3. **Analyze** it: explain how its language supports your point.

The most common weakness is the "dropped quotation," a quotation followed by no analysis. A good rule: for every line you quote, write at least two lines of analysis.

### Worked example: integrating evidence

> When Mrs. Mallard finally whispers "free, free, free!" (Chopin), the repetition does more than express joy. Each repetition seems to test the word, as if she is speaking it for the first time; the exclamation, set off and unexplained, suggests a feeling that has no place in the respectable language of widowhood. Chopin lets the word stand alone because, in Mrs. Mallard's world, no sentence exists that could hold it.

Notice the move from quotation to close analysis of form (repetition, punctuation, placement) to interpretation.

## Literary present tense

Write about literature in the **present tense**: Mrs. Mallard *sits* by the window; Glaspell *shows* the women's understanding. The events of a text happen whenever it is read.

## Structure

1. **Introduction:** engage the reader, introduce the work and author, and state your thesis.
2. **Body paragraphs:** each begins with a claim that advances the thesis, supported by quoted evidence and analysis. Organize by idea, not by plot order.
3. **Counterpoint:** address a complication or alternative reading.
4. **Conclusion:** show what your argument reveals about the work as a whole and why it matters.

## MLA citation

Literary studies typically use **MLA style**. In-text citations are brief, usually the author and page number in parentheses, e.g., (Chopin 3). For poems, cite line numbers; for plays, act, scene, and line numbers where available. A **Works Cited** list at the end gives full publication information for each source. Consult the current MLA Handbook for exact formats.

## Joining the conversation

When you write a research essay, you engage **secondary sources**, scholarship by critics. Use them to support, extend, or argue against. Never let critics replace your own argument; your voice should lead. The templates in Gerald Graff and Cathy Birkenstein's *They Say / I Say* ("Although some critics argue X, a closer look at Y suggests Z") capture the basic move of academic writing: responding to what others have said.

## Academic integrity

Paraphrasing a critic's argument without citing it, or submitting AI-generated interpretations as your own, misrepresents your work. The point of writing about literature is to develop your own reading. Your interpretation, grounded in the text, is what matters.

## Course synthesis

You've learned to read closely; to analyze plot, character, point of view, setting, theme, and symbol; to read drama; to weigh context; and to write arguments about literature. These are the tools you'll use throughout the program, from Shakespeare to contemporary fiction.

## Common misconceptions

- **"A good essay summarizes the plot."** Assume your reader knows the plot; argue about meaning.
- **"More quotations make a stronger essay."** Analysis, not quantity, makes evidence persuasive.
- **"Critics' views are more valid than mine."** Your reading, supported by evidence, contributes to the conversation.

## Summary

A literary essay argues a specific, arguable thesis about a text. Quotations must be introduced, precise, and analyzed. Write in the literary present tense, organize by idea, address complications, cite in MLA style, and engage critics while keeping your own argument central.
